chunks: "A differential pair is two conductors that carry the same signal with opposite polarity.
The driver pushes one wire up while it pulls the other down by the same amount, around some common-mode level.
The receiver looks only at the difference between the two wires, V-plus minus V-minus, and ignores what they have in common. That's what makes it work well.
Any noise that couples onto the pair, from a neighbouring trace, a ground shift, or a magnetic field, hits both wires about equally, because they run side by side.
So it shows up as common-mode, and the differential receiver subtracts it away. The signal, in contrast, is opposite on the two wires, so the subtraction doubles it.
Other benefits: the two currents are equal and opposite, so the return path is the other wire, which means less loop area, less EMI and less ground bounce.
The receiver's threshold is built in, the crossing point between the two wires, so it doesn't depend on a ground reference.

In practice it's terminated across the pair, about 100 ohms, and the two wires need to stay matched in length and symmetric, because any skew or imbalance turns common-mode into differential and eats the benefit.
The cost is two pins and two traces per signal."
